text: Rain is coming. We need to repair the roof. One board is broken. Replace that board, but keep the dry boards. A cloth cover is only a temporary solution.

The cottage stayed dry last night, but one roof board has cracked. We should repair the roof before the next shower. Replace only the damaged board; the other boards are still reliable. A cloth cover may help for an hour, but it is only a temporary solution. Save the sound wood for the porch.
Replace the broken board. Keep the dry wood beside the cottage.
The boat will deliver wood today. Gather the loose stones from the path. Rope is scarce, so repairing the landing area is our first priority. The flowers can wait.

A boat will deliver fresh wood this afternoon. Before it arrives, gather the loose stones that block the path. Rope is scarce, and we cannot repair every corner today. Our priority is a safe landing area. Once the crew can reach the cottage without slipping, we can return to the flower beds.
Clear the path first. Then carry the new wood to the landing area.
An ordinary chair sits beneath the porch. Its frame is strong. We can restore the seat and preserve the frame. Do not throw the whole chair away.

We found an ordinary wooden chair beneath the porch. The seat has worn out, but the frame is still strong. Instead of throwing the chair away, restore its seat and preserve the useful frame. It will give the boat crew a comfortable place to rest. Keep the chair under the roof so that rain cannot reach it.
Put the repaired chair beneath the porch, away from the rain.
Two friends will visit. Adapt the porch to accommodate them. A versatile folding table leaves room for a bench. We can expand the porch later; today, move the large crates.

Two friends are arriving on the next boat. We can adapt the porch to accommodate them without rebuilding the cottage. A versatile folding table can serve both meals and repairs. Move the large crates inside to make space for a bench. If more visitors arrive later, we can expand the porch, but there is no need to do everything today.
Move the crates inside. Leave enough space for the bench.
The mill turns slowly. The rough surface of one part causes friction. Make it smooth to reduce friction. Avoid the moving sails while you work. Stop the mill first.

The wind is strong enough, yet the mill turns slowly. A rough surface inside the mechanism is rubbing against another part. We can reduce friction by making that surface smooth. To avoid an accident, stop the sails before opening the cover. Adding more weight will not solve the problem; careful repair will.
Stop the sails. Smooth the rough surface before starting the mill again.
We can obtain water from the pump. The small tank has limited capacity. Use an efficient pipe with no leaks. One full tank is adequate for the garden today.

The new pump helps us obtain water from the shore. However, the storage tank has a limited capacity. An efficient system needs a sealed pipe so that water reaches the tank instead of leaking onto the path. One full tank is adequate for today. When it is full, close the valve rather than letting the water overflow.
Fill the tank, then close the valve. Save the water for the garden.
A storm is coming. The tall support is fragile. Reinforce it so the mill can withstand the wind. Our main constraint is time. Repair the support before painting the door.

The next storm may bring stronger winds. A fragile support beneath the mill needs attention if the structure is to withstand the weather. Reinforce the support with the spare beams. Our main constraint is time, so painting the door must wait. Strengthening the part that carries the load matters more than changing its colour.
Use the spare beams to reinforce the support. Paint the door later.
Wind speed can fluctuate. A tank helps sustain the water supply when the wind stops. Stored water can mitigate a short shortage and keep the supply consistent. Fill the tank while the mill runs.

Wind speed can fluctuate throughout the day. The garden needs a more consistent supply of water than the weather can provide on its own. A storage tank helps sustain the supply during calm periods. Keeping some water in reserve can mitigate a short shortage. Fill the tank while the mill is running, and use the stored water when the sails stop.
Store water while the wind blows. Use the reserve when the sails stop.
Seeds are abundant, but sunny space is scarce. Gather the empty pots. Space is a useful resource. Leave a gap between the pots so that every plant can receive light.

We have abundant seeds, but space in the sunny corner is scarce. Gather the empty pots before deciding where to put them. Space is a resource too: packing every pot into one tight row will leave some plants in shade. Leave a small gap between the pots and keep the taller plants behind the shorter ones.
Leave a gap between the pots. Put the tall plants at the back.
Water is essential for the seedlings. Cover the soil with dry leaves to retain moisture. Add roughly one thin layer. Growth is gradual, so do not dig up the roots every morning.

The seedlings need water, but the soil dries quickly in the sun. A thin layer of dry leaves can help it retain moisture. Add roughly enough leaves to cover the bare surface without burying the stems. Water remains essential, and growth will be gradual. Check the soil gently instead of disturbing the roots every morning.
Cover the bare soil with a thin layer of leaves. Keep the stems clear.
We must allocate water between two beds. Give a larger proportion to the dry bed. Replenish the tank afterwards. Otherwise, there will be no water for the evening.

One garden bed is much drier than the other. We need to allocate the remaining water carefully rather than give both beds the same amount. Send a larger proportion to the dry bed, then replenish the tank while the wind is still strong. Otherwise, we may have nothing left for the young plants in the evening.
Water the dry bed first. Replenish the tank before the wind drops.
The older plants are resilient. The young seedlings are susceptible to cold. Anticipate a chilly night and cover only the young plants. Leaving them outside may have a serious consequence.

The weather report suggests a cold night. The older plants are resilient, but the young seedlings are susceptible to sudden changes in temperature. We can anticipate the problem and move the youngest pots beneath the shelter. Leaving every plant exposed may have a serious consequence. Keep the cover loose enough to let air pass through.
Move the young seedlings beneath the shelter. Leave a small gap for air.
We can expand the island beside the shore. Keep each new surface close to the old land. A gradual change leaves a short distance for the worker to cross.

We can expand the island beside the shore. Keep each new surface close to the old land. A gradual change leaves a short distance for the worker to cross. Start with the nearest section, then connect the next one. The trees can remain where they are. There is no need to clear the whole forest before making a path.
Connect the nearest section first, and leave the trees beside the path.
The sawmill turns short logs into boards. Keep the surface clear and move one log at a time. This is efficient: it can reduce waste and preserve useful pieces.

The sawmill turns short logs into boards. Keep the surface clear and move one log at a time. This is efficient: it can reduce waste and preserve useful pieces. Put the finished boards beside the table, away from the moving blade. Later, the boards will form the cottage floor and the narrow path beside the water.
Place the finished boards beside the table, away from the moving blade.
Gather stone for the kiln base. The thick walls retain heat, but the front opening must remain clear. Be patient after firing. Avoid moving the bricks while they are hot.

Gather stone for the kiln base. The thick walls retain heat, but the front opening must remain clear. Be patient after firing. Avoid moving the bricks while they are hot. Leave a small space between each row so air can pass through. Once the bricks cool, carry them to the new garden wall and the windmill base.
Leave the front opening clear, and wait for the bricks to cool.
The meadow has room for a garden and a path. Allocate adequate space between them. Our choice matters: the worker must still reach the small hill beyond the garden.

The meadow has room for a garden and a path. Allocate adequate space between them. Our choice matters: the worker must still reach the small hill beyond the garden. Put the new beds on one side instead of across the middle. Flowers can grow along the edge, while the open path connects the old shore to the new ground.
Place the beds on one side, and keep the middle path open.
Notice the pale crystals in the dark stone. Distinguish the loose pieces from the large cluster. The points are fragile, so preserve the cluster and collect the loose pieces first.

Notice the pale crystals in the dark stone. Distinguish the loose pieces from the large cluster. The points are fragile, so preserve the cluster and collect the loose pieces first. A heavy blow could break several points at once. Use a small tool near the base. Leave the tallest crystal as a bright feature of the new bay.
Collect the loose pieces first, and leave the tallest crystal in place.
Gather boards, strong cloth, and iron parts for the new boat. Fit the boards first, then add the cloth sail. Keep the iron parts in a dry box beside the boat.

Gather boards, strong cloth, and iron parts for the new boat. Fit the boards first, then add the cloth sail. Keep the iron parts in a dry box beside the boat. Use them to reinforce the places where the boards meet. Check the bottom for gaps before moving the boat into the water. A careful repair now helps make the boat reliable.
Fit the boards first, then add the cloth sail. Keep the iron parts dry.
We sail to the green islands for hard wood and fruit. Follow the bright flags along the shore. Leave some fruit on each tree so the birds still have food.

We sail to the green islands for hard wood and fruit. Follow the bright flags along the shore. Leave some fruit on each tree so the birds still have food. Tie the boat beside the steps before carrying anything aboard. Gather fallen wood near the path, and keep the fruit in a basket away from wet ropes.
Follow the flags along the shore, and leave some fruit for the birds.
Collect the pale sea glass beside the rocks. Wash off the sand, then rub each piece until the surface is smooth. Only clear pieces can become lenses for the telescope.

Collect the pale sea glass beside the rocks. Wash off the sand, then rub each piece until the surface is smooth. Only clear pieces can become lenses for the telescope. Put cloudy pieces in a separate tray. They can decorate the workshop instead. Hold a finished lens toward the sky and check whether a distant tree looks clear.
Keep the clear glass for lenses, and put the cloudy pieces in the tray.
The black shore has strong stone that can withstand water. Carry small blocks to the work table. Shape them into short pipes, and smooth the edges before joining the pieces.

The black shore has strong stone that can withstand water. Carry small blocks to the work table. Shape them into short pipes, and smooth the edges before joining the pieces. Leave a round opening through each pipe so water can pass. Check the joints for gaps. Keep finished pipes beside the path, ready for the new water station.
Smooth the edges of each pipe before joining the pieces.
The tide wheel turns as the water moves. Connect the stone pipes before opening the gate. Then follow the water along the channel to check that it reaches the garden.

The tide wheel turns as the water moves. Connect the stone pipes before opening the gate. Then follow the water along the channel to check that it reaches the garden. If a joint leaks, close the gate and repair it. Keep leaves away from the wheel. The small pool beside the garden can hold water while the wheel rests.
Close the gate before repairing the pipe, then open it again when the joint is secure.
A red scarf is on the last seat of the bus. A child points at it. The driver puts it in a box beside her seat.

A red scarf is on the last seat of the bus. A child points at it. The driver puts it in a box beside her seat. At the next stop, an old man runs back to the bus. He touches his neck and smiles when the driver opens the box.
Leave the scarf with the driver so the man can find it.
My sister likes cold tea. I like mine hot. I put a small spoon by my cup and a piece of ice in hers.
My sister likes cold tea. I like mine hot. I put a small spoon by my cup and a piece of ice in hers. The cups look the same from the door. She picks the one with the ice and carries it to the window.
Take the cup with the ice and leave the spoon here.
A little bird lands on the window. I reach for my camera, but the bird is gone. Its feet have left two small marks in the snow.

A little bird lands on the window. I reach for my camera, but the bird is gone. Its feet have left two small marks in the snow. I take a picture of the marks instead. Later my brother asks why I took a picture of an empty window.
Look at the snow before you close the window.
The drummer taps four times before the song. On the fourth tap, the singer takes a breath. Both start together just after that last tap.

The drummer taps four times before the song. On the fourth tap, the singer takes a breath. Both start together just after that last tap. At first I thought the taps were part of the song. During practice the singer listened to them even when nobody else was playing.
Listen for four taps, then begin the first line.
I fell asleep on the train. When I woke up, the sea was on the wrong side. I had passed my stop and the train was turning around the bay.

I fell asleep on the train. When I woke up, the sea was on the wrong side. I had passed my stop and the train was turning around the bay. A woman showed me the stops on her map. There was another train back in twenty minutes, so I had time to look at the water.
Get off at the next stop and take the train back.
There is no picture in the letter from my friend. Instead there is a yellow leaf. She writes that the tree outside her new room is taller than the roof.

There is no picture in the letter from my friend. Instead there is a yellow leaf. She writes that the tree outside her new room is taller than the roof. I put the leaf between two pages of my book. Now I can picture the window even though I have never seen her street.
Keep the leaf between the pages so it stays flat.
Our team only needed one more point. I was close to the basket, but a tall player stood in front of me. I passed the ball to a friend behind him.

Our team only needed one more point. I was close to the basket, but a tall player stood in front of me. I passed the ball to a friend behind him. For a second the tall player kept watching my hands. By the time he turned, the ball was already in the air.
Pass the ball behind the tall player before he turns.
In the film, we hear rain before we see the dark clouds. At the studio there was no water at all. Someone shook a box of rice beside the microphone.

In the film, we hear rain before we see the dark clouds. At the studio there was no water at all. Someone shook a box of rice beside the microphone. When the picture disappeared, the sound suddenly seemed dry and light. With the street back on the screen, it felt like rain again.
Start the rain sound before the clouds appear on screen.
At breakfast I put a stick in the sand and marked the end of its shadow. At lunch the mark was still there, but the shadow ended much closer to the stick.

At breakfast I put a stick in the sand and marked the end of its shadow. At lunch the mark was still there, but the shadow ended much closer to the stick. I checked the stick first. It had not moved. The clear sky made the second mark easy to draw, so I stayed to make one more before dinner.
Mark the end of the shadow without moving the stick.
In our game, each player could carry one lamp. We needed both hands to open the final door. I put my lamp on the floor while my friend held hers above the lock.

In our game, each player could carry one lamp. We needed both hands to open the final door. I put my lamp on the floor while my friend held hers above the lock. The light on the floor showed the steps behind us. That mattered a minute later when we had to find our way back in a hurry.
Hold your lamp over the lock while I open the door.
The cafe offered a cheaper drink to customers who brought a cup. More people came, yet fewer seats were free. Most of the new customers stayed to chat after finishing their drinks.

The cafe offered a cheaper drink to customers who brought a cup. More people came, yet fewer seats were free. Most of the new customers stayed to chat after finishing their drinks. The owner had expected to save money on paper cups. She had not expected the room itself to become the scarce part of the business.
Offer the discount for a cup, but count the empty seats as well.
A museum counted its visitors by collecting a ticket from each person at the door. One evening the ticket total was lower than the number on the camera. A guide had entered twice with the same group.

A museum counted its visitors by collecting a ticket from each person at the door. One evening the ticket total was lower than the number on the camera. A guide had entered twice with the same group. The camera counted both visits, while the guide handed over a ticket only once. Before changing the numbers, the manager asked what each system was actually counting.
Compare the two counts before deciding which number to report.
